title: The Postman's Fifty Centimes That Helped Build the Institut Pasteur
dek: In 1886 Louis Pasteur chose to fund a rabies institute by public subscription rather than the state, and turned down the city's land to stay independent.

story.event: Funding a rabies treatment and research institute by international public subscription
story.summary: On 1 March 1886 Louis Pasteur reported to the French Academy of Sciences that of 350 people given his rabies treatment one had died, and called for a rabies vaccine centre; the Academy's committee launched an international public subscription on 14 March. Pasteur intended the institute to be funded by donations rather than the state, and declined a plot offered by Paris City Council in favour of an independent site. The Institut Pasteur received charitable status on 4 June 1887 and was opened by President Sadi Carnot on 14 November 1888, with about 2.59 million francs raised.
paragraphs: On 1 March 1886, Louis Pasteur, then 63, told the French Academy of Sciences what had happened since the previous July, when he first treated Joseph Meister, a nine-year-old boy bitten by a rabid dog. Of 350 people given his rabies treatment, one had died. "A rabies vaccine center should be set up," he concluded. Bitten people were arriving at his laboratory from across Europe, among them nineteen Russians mauled by a wolf.

He had already decided how such a centre should be paid for. When a philanthropist sent 40,000 francs, Pasteur said he meant to build a model establishment funded by donations and an international subscription, without turning to the state, though he wanted to wait until the treatment's success was beyond doubt. The Academy's committee agreed unanimously, and the appeal opened on 14 March. Doubt remained: three of the Russians died, and critics dwelt on failures. Historians who later read his notebooks found that some of his published results had claimed more than his private records showed.

The Journal Officiel printed lists in which the Tsar of Russia, who gave 100,000 francs, and the Emperor of Brazil appeared beside a policeman giving one franc and a postman giving fifty centimes. Joseph Meister's name was on a list from Alsace-Lorraine. By April the fund had passed 500,000 francs. The strain told: that autumn, with signs of heart trouble, his doctors persuaded him to rest for the winter on the Italian Riviera.

The harder choice concerned land. Paris City Council, after heated debate, offered a plot on the rue Vauquelin that he was already using. Pasteur turned it down, writing in January 1887 that a laboratory scientist would prefer a more modest but independent home. In March, with the appeal nearing two million francs, his committee bought land in Vaugirard, and a decree of 4 June 1887 gave the Institut Pasteur charitable status.

President Sadi Carnot opened it on 14 November 1888. The treasurer's accounts, which also recorded a 200,000-franc grant from parliament, showed 2,586,680 francs raised, leaving more than a million as an endowment. Overcome, Pasteur had his son read his speech, which said the building held no stone that was not the sign of a generous thought.

quote.text: liberality resides not in the multitude of the gifts but in the state of character of the giver, and this is relative to the giver's substance. There is therefore nothing to prevent the man who gives less from being the more liberal man, if he has less to give
quote.source_title: Nicomachean Ethics, tr. W. D. Ross, The Internet Classics Archive (MIT)
quote.connection: The subscription printed a tsar's 100,000 francs beside a postman's fifty centimes. Aristotle explains why the small gift is not a footnote: generosity is measured against what the giver has, so the poorer subscriber may well have been the more generous of the two.

reflection: The lists in the Journal Officiel are the part of this story worth keeping. An emperor's gift and a postman's fifty centimes were printed on the same pages and counted in the same total. Aristotle would have understood: he measured generosity against what the giver had, not against the size of the gift.

That measure works in both directions for you. Some of the help you receive comes from people with little to spare: a colleague's half hour, a relative's patience with your late evenings. And on the days when your own energy is low, what you can give is smaller. By Aristotle's reckoning, that does not make it less.

cross_checks.claim: On 1 March 1886 Pasteur reported 350 people treated with one death and called for a rabies vaccine institute
Pasteur intended the institute to be funded by donations and an international subscription rather than by the state
The international subscription drew gifts from the Tsar of Russia and the Emperor of Brazil alongside small donors
The subscription raised about 2.5 million francs or more (2,586,680 francs by the treasurer's account at the opening)
President Sadi Carnot opened the Institut Pasteur on 14 November 1888

research_notes: Totals agree: the Institut Pasteur's timeline gives more than 2.5 million gold francs by January 1888, and the treasurer's statement at the November 1888 opening, as reported by Vallery-Radot, gives 2,586,680 francs. Vallery-Radot then says the French Chambers had voted 200,000 francs and international gifts had been added, without making clear whether the parliamentary grant is inside or outside the 2,586,680 total, so the story says only that the accounts also recorded the grant. That grant sits awkwardly with Pasteur's stated aim of not relying on the state; the story reports both, and funding is set to nonprofit because the institute was founded as a privately funded foundation with charitable status. The 350-treated, one-death figure comes from Pasteur's own report to the Academy, quoted by both the Institut Pasteur and Vallery-Radot; the Science History Institute notes that his notebooks show he altered or exaggerated results in landmark publications and that later accounts questioned his claimed dog trials, so the story says historians later found some published results claimed more than his private records showed, rather than treating his 1886 figures as settled. The Tsar's 100,000 francs comes from Vallery-Radot only; the Institut Pasteur names the Tsar as a donor without an amount. The line 'A rabies vaccine center should be set up' is the Institut Pasteur's English translation of Pasteur's words (Vallery-Radot's translator renders it 'It is advisable to create a vaccinal institute against hydrophobia'); its US spelling is kept as quoted. The closing speech line is paraphrased from both translations. Vallery-Radot was Pasteur's son-in-law, so his book is used for documented events, letters and speeches rather than judgements. The Institut Pasteur gives the Vaugirard plot as 11,000 square metres and Vallery-Radot as 11,000 square yards; the story gives no area. Joseph Meister's age (nine) is given by the Institut Pasteur and the Science History Institute. The 'Italian Riviera' is Bordighera, where Vallery-Radot says Pasteur wintered from late November 1886.
